research_text:
## Research brief

### API and finding

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and acts as a factory for socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances. Its initialization supplies key managers, trust managers and a source of randomness. The reported finding concerns the **first argument** to `SSLContext.init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)`: the array supplying local authentication keys. It describes an analysis finding about that array, not a documented runtime exception or proof that a manager is defective. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))

Official API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html

### Documented usage and remediation

- Oracle documents initializing a newly created context and permits either factory-created managers or implementations of the manager interfaces. A documented factory approach is to initialize a `KeyManagerFactory` from key material and obtain its array with `getKeyManagers()`. This is a documented way to supply factory-produced managers; Oracle does **not** say that every directly implemented key manager is invalid or prescribe one universal remediation for this detector finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))
- The API permits null arguments. Its description says providers are searched for an appropriate factory when a manager argument is null. The JSSE guide separately says a null key-manager array results in an **empty key manager**, and distinguishes that from the internal default context’s default key manager. These descriptions should not be treated as a guarantee that null supplies the same local credentials as an explicitly configured factory. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- The first instance of a particular manager implementation type in an array is used. Trust decisions and endpoint identification are separate concerns; changing key-manager provenance does not by itself establish either. `SSLParameters` documents endpoint-identification configuration. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

JSSE guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html  
KeyManagerFactory API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html

### Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted formats:** The cited `SSLContext` and factory documentation does not specify a persisted-format change or a keystore-conversion migration merely because the key-manager array comes from a factory. A factory can use a `KeyStore` or provider-specific key sources. Compatibility still depends on the actual key material and provider; these sources do not establish compatibility for a particular store. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))
- **Wire formats:** The factory provenance predicate does not itself specify a TLS wire-format change. If a usage change also changes the negotiated protocol or credentials, compatibility is a separate matter. Oracle notes that TLS 1.3 is not directly compatible with earlier versions, and identifies differences including cipher suites, certificate signature support and connection closing. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Platform support:** Java SE 26 requires implementations to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3` context protocols; the Java SE 11 API’s required list does not include `TLSv1.3`. Oracle documents TLS 1.3 implementation in JDK 8u261, with release-specific client defaults. Support and defaults must therefore be checked for the target runtime and provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Protocol distinction:** The CrySL literals constrain the requested `getInstance` name, not the protocol ultimately enabled or negotiated. Oracle’s standard names say even a version-specific context name may support other TLS versions. Conversely, `getInstance("TLS")` alone does not establish that a legacy version will be negotiated. The sources document protocol configuration mechanisms, but do not prescribe pinning a context name solely to satisfy this finding. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Oracle compatibility guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html  
Standard names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html

### Exact CrySL rule

The supplied source declares the following relevant clauses verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext
```

```text
i1: init(km, tm, random);
Init := i1;
```

```text
REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl

The source declares a rule for **`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`**, not a name-only rule over arbitrary receiver types. Its `init` event specifies three parameters: the declared `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]` and `SecureRandom`. The relevant condition is the required predicate `generatedKeyManagers[km]`, alongside the two other displayed requirements. **A method on an unrelated type merely sharing the name `init` is not a match under the rule as declared.** The file does not itself document every receiver-resolution detail of a particular analyzer implementation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The same file declares one- and two-argument `getInstance` events, zero- and two-argument `createSSLEngine` events, and a forbidden `getDefault()` event. Its order is `Get, Init, Engine?`; it constrains the requested protocol string to `TLSv1.2` or `TLSv1.3`. It contains no event for a handshake or enabled-protocol configuration. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Source limits:** The rule’s predicate is an analysis requirement, not a guarantee of correct credential selection or peer validation. The supplied URL points to a mutable branch; the provided SHA-256 was not independently verified here against the retrieved bytes. The compiled rule artifact and detector version are also unavailable, so their exact matching and diagnostic behavior remain unresolved.
